8.0.s.en: 1. A basket for the bitter gathering:

8.0.0.en: 1 Thus hath the Lord GOD shewed unto me: and behold a basket of summer fruit. 2 And he said, "Amos, what seest thou?" And I said, "A basket of summer fruit." Then said the LORD unto me, "The end is come upon my people of Israel; I will not again pass by them any more. 3 And the songs of the temple shall be howlings in that day, saith the Lord GOD: there shall be many dead bodies in every place; they shall cast them forth with silence."

8.0.1.en: God showed him a basket for gathering; in Hebrew the word means "fruit at the end of summer or in the autumn." The time had come to eat the fruit, but it is not joyful fruit; it is the ripened fruit of sin, which cannot be waited upon. The time of dark winter had drawn near, and it was necessary to eat the fruit that does not remain for the winter!

8.1.0.en: God gave them many opportunities to repent of their sins and return to Him, at one time by declarations, at another by gifts and kindnesses, and at a third by threats... He used to chastise so that He might return and forgive, but now they have prepared themselves for destruction... "The end is come upon my people of Israel" [2]. He does not forget that they are His people, but their end has come because of their persistence in their evil, as He says: "I will not again pass by them any more" [2]. The songs of the palace (the temple) and their joys turn into mourning and weeping, and instead of joy corpses without number are gathered in silence, when they see the temple become a ruin and the distress too great to be borne, or because they find no strength to weep for the multitude of the dead; and perhaps the silence is also a sign of fear of the enemy, lest he hear their voices and come and kill the remnant that is left!

8.1.1.en: Though God is very longsuffering, as the Apostle says: "Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance? But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God; who will render to every man according to his deeds" (Rom 2:4-6).

8.1.2.en: God in His love watches in us for a sign toward Him so that He may return to us; He longs to dwell in us and to enter with us into His glories. But if we hold fast to refusal and walk in evil, our sins ripen to be gathered as in the bitter basket of gathering, which the Lord cannot bear, and our end comes though we are His children, and our sonship to Him becomes a secret of torment for the soul and a testimony of judgment, and instead of songs of joy it becomes a wailing of the soul, which finds the temple emptied and everything within it of gifts and endowments finished! Let us then return to Him and He will return to us, that we may have within us His joyful paradise instead of this sorrowful basket!

8.2.0.en: 4 Hear this, O ye that swallow up the needy, even to make the poor of the land to fail, 5 Saying, "When will the new moon be gone, that we may sell corn? and the sabbath, that we may set forth wheat, making the ephah small, and the shekel great, and falsifying the balances by deceit? 6 That we may buy the poor for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes; yea, and sell the refuse of the wheat?" 7 The LORD hath sworn by the excellency of Jacob, "Surely I will never forget any of their works. 8 Shall not the land tremble for this, and every one mourn that dwelleth therein? and it shall rise up wholly as a flood; and it shall be cast out and drowned, as by the flood of Egypt. 9 And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the Lord GOD, that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day: 10 And I will turn your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation; and I will bring up sackcloth upon all loins, and baldness upon every head; and I will make it as the mourning of an only son, and the end thereof as a bitter day."

8.2.1.en: The prophet presents to us a picture of the state of injustice and corruption in which Israel lived at that time. Among its features:

8.2.2.en: First: he says, "Hear this, O ye that swallow up the needy, even to make the poor of the land to fail" [4]. They want to crush the poor; they long to swallow them in their bellies or trample them under their feet, to make the poor of the land to fail. In their love of themselves they permit themselves injustice, even the utter destruction of the poor and needy by every means, for the sake of their wealth, their belly and their revelry!

8.2.3.en: When the ego swells, a person thinks himself the center of the world; everyone works for his account and everyone perishes for the sake of his happiness. But of the Lord of glory Jesus it was said: "For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich" (2 Cor 8:9). When we carry Him in us we are enriched by Him, and the sign of our riches is that we accept to become poor with Him so that our brethren may be enriched by Christ who dwells in us. We long to be enslaved so that they may be freed in Him, to die so that they may enjoy life with Him, and to leave everything so that they may possess it as the secret of their wealth. Thus our teacher the Apostle Paul walked in the spirit of his Master when he said: "For though I be free from all men, yet have I made myself servant unto all, that I might gain the more" (1 Cor 9:20), "For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake" (2 Cor 4:5).

8.3.0.en: Second: "Saying, When will the new moon be gone, that we may sell corn? and the sabbath, that we may set forth wheat" [5]. They fulfill the Law to the letter and stop work on the new moon and every sabbath, as though they were religious and lovers of God, but these days pass over them very heavily, for they long for them to pass so that they may return to their trade and material gain. In the eyes of people, and perhaps in their own eyes, they are righteous, hallowing the feast days and sabbaths, but their heart in reality is not sanctified, for it is occupied with profit and matter, even if work has stopped outwardly! As it was said: "For with their mouth they shew much love, but their heart goeth after their covetousness" (Ezek 33:31).

8.3.1.en: It is a painful picture of the soul that has become earth, which finds the day of the Lord burdensome, and feels in worship that it is long and without profit, while it spends most of its time rejoicing in material gains!

8.3.2.en: Third: "Making the ephah small, and the shekel great, and falsifying the balances by deceit" [5]. It is said in Proverbs, "A false balance is abomination to the LORD" (Prov 11:1).

8.3.3.en: Some explain their making the ephah small and the shekel great as meaning that they sell to people by the ephah and cheat them by making it smaller than it ought to be, and when they buy wholesale they buy by the shekel, and make it larger to cheat the farmers who sell to them. It is as though they steal in their dealings, in buying as in selling, for their own account.

8.4.0.en: Fourth: "That we may buy the poor for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes; yea, and sell the refuse of the wheat" [6]. In our study of the second chapter the Lord says: "They sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for a pair of shoes" (Amos 2:6), and we saw that in reality they sell the Lord, the only Righteous One, for the sake of material things, and they despise Him in the person of the poor and needy for a pair of shoes. He had earlier commanded Moses to take them off (Ex 3), and the disciples not to acquire them (Mt 10:10).

8.4.1.en: They buy the weak for silver; when the poor fell into extreme misery they would go to the rich of their own people and sell themselves and their children to them as slaves for the price of food, so that they might be able to live, a matter that later stirred up Nehemiah (Neh 5).

8.4.2.en: As for their selling the refuse of the wheat, in it is a violation of the Law and a removal of love, for it ought to have been left for the poor who cannot afford to buy wheat to enjoy, so that they might take the refuse. On this principle it is written in the book of Deuteronomy: "When thou cuttest down thine harvest in thy field, and hast forgot a sheaf in the field, thou shalt not go again to fetch it: it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow: that the LORD thy God may bless thee in all the work of thine hands..." (Deut 24:19).

8.5.0.en: When Israel, the people of God, reached this bitter state, it fell under severe trial, as the prophet says: "The LORD hath sworn by the excellency of Jacob, Surely I will never forget any of their works. Shall not the land tremble for this, and every one mourn that dwelleth therein? and it shall rise up wholly as a flood; and it shall be cast out and drowned, as by the flood of Egypt. And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the Lord GOD, that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day: and I will turn your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation; and I will bring up sackcloth upon all loins, and baldness upon every head; and I will make it as the mourning of an only son, and the end thereof as a bitter day" [7-10].

8.5.1.en: With all the injustice and iniquity that Israel committed, so that the Lord swore He would never forget any of these evil works of theirs, that is, He would forgive no more, He still holds a special affection for them, for He says: "The LORD hath sworn by the excellency of Jacob"... We are His children; He boasts of us and longs for our salvation despite what we have done and the wrong we have done to Him.

8.5.2.en: Before the injustice of this people the whole land trembled and its inhabitants mourned, and it rose up as a flood and began to shake as in an earthquake, like the River Nile which overflows with water at the time of the flood and then its water falls again! The sun cannot look upon this evil, so it goes down at noon and the earth turns to darkness instead of light, and the feasts are turned into mourning and the songs into lamentations, and people put on sackcloth instead of adornment, and become like one who has lost his only son, in bitter anguish.

8.5.3.en: It is a natural bitter fruit tasted by the one whose cup is filled with evil, for his land, that is, his body that offers him pleasures, trembles before God and loses its vitality, and all its inhabitants mourn, that is, his senses and feelings lose all joy, to enter a state of despair and discontent; a person's life shakes as in an earthquake, and he becomes like the Nile of Egypt, constantly rising and falling without stability. The Sun of Righteousness sets for him, so he loses all the enlightenment he had once enjoyed, and his inner land turns into the gloom of ignorance. He does not know spiritual joy, but his inner feasts turn into a funeral, and instead of praise he utters lamentations, and instead of inner spiritual adornment he is in disgrace like one who wears sackcloth. His life turns like that of one at a funeral, so he shaves the hair of his head to become bald, and weeps like one who has lost his only son, who is his own one soul!

8.5.4.en: And the wonder is that the Lord carried this bitter fruit for us when He bowed His back to the Cross, "and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all" (Isa 53:6). So this prophecy was fulfilled literally. The earth trembled, as the Evangelist says: "And the earth did quake, and the rocks rent; and the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints which slept arose" (Mt 27:51-52).

8.5.5.en: The earth quaked, and Hades also quaked. And the sun went down at noon, as the same Evangelist says: "Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour" (Mt 27:45). And the feasts of the Jews were afterwards turned into mourning and their songs into lamentations, since they lost the temple and were scattered through all the lands and lost their position as the people of God, so they became like those in the mourning for an only son.

8.5.6.en: Many of the Fathers saw in these words a striking prophecy of what happened during the Passion of the Lord Christ, among them Father Lactantius, Tertullian the teacher, and St. Irenaeus.

8.5.7.en: St. Irenaeus says: [He announced clearly that the eclipse of the sun at the time of His crucifixion would take place at the sixth hour and after (Amos 8:9); after this their feasts according to the Law and their songs would be turned into sorrow and wailing when they are delivered to the Gentiles.] In the same sense Tertullian the teacher says: [You were taken captive and scattered after the Passion of Christ, as the Holy Spirit had foretold.] As Isaiah also says: "I clothe the heavens with blackness" (Isa 50:3). This is the day of which Amos writes: "And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the Lord GOD, that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day." For at noon the veil of the temple was rent, as the cherubim fled (Ezek 11:22-23), when "the daughter of Zion is left as a cottage in a vineyard, as a lodge in a garden of cucumbers" (Isa 1:8)].

8.5.8.en: St. John Chrysostom gives a spiritual understanding, in our daily life, of the eclipse of the sun and the coming of darkness upon the earth, saying: [It seems to me that not only the earth, but even the nature of the air and the circle of the sun's rays look on with sorrow, so that its rays became all the more clouded (dark), not because its elements have changed, but because our eyes are troubled with clouds of sorrow and have become unable to see the light of the rays clearly... This is what the prophet wept over long ago when he said: "I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day." He says this not because the planet of the day was eclipsed or the day disappeared, but because those who are in sorrow cannot perceive the light of noon because of the darkness of their blindness.] We need God to remove from us the darkness of sin, so that our eyes may be enlightened by His Holy Spirit to behold Jesus Christ the Sun of Righteousness and to enjoy His splendor in us!

8.5.9.en: As for the turning of the feasts into sorrow and the songs into mourning, this is the natural work of sin, while repentance gives us the opposite in Christ Jesus, for to Him we return, and in Him we find our feast truly joyful and delightful. As St. Gregory the Wonderworker says: [It is our duty to keep this feast, seeing that it fills the whole world with joy and gladness. Let us keep it with psalms, hymns and spiritual songs... Our Lord has assured us that He turns our sorrows into joy through the fruit of repentance.]

8.6.s.en: 3. A famine for the words of the Lord:

8.6.0.en: 11 "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD: 12 And they shall wander from sea to sea, and from the north even to the east, they shall run to and fro to seek the word of the LORD, and shall not find it. 13 In that day shall the fair virgins and young men faint for thirst. 14 They that swear by the sin of Samaria, and say, Thy god, O Dan, liveth; and, The manner of Beersheba liveth; even they shall fall, and never rise up again."

8.6.1.en: The fruit of sin is shattering from every side: a bodily shattering, where the land trembles and every one mourns that dwelleth therein [8]; a psychological shattering, where the soul loses its light and turns into a state of gloom and is in unceasing mourning; and finally a spiritual shattering, where a person loses his spiritual food, as He says: "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD... In that day shall the fair virgins and young men faint for thirst" [11-13].

8.7.0.en: This is what God threatens the wicked with: that they enter into a hunger and thirst not for bread and water but for the life-giving words of the Lord. They wander from sea to sea, that is, from a teacher marked by the temporal character, for the sea refers to the world with its troubled waves; they seek satisfaction for their souls and peace from teachers who are deprived of spiritual satisfaction and true peace; they search in all parts of the world from the north to the south... but in vain, until all their gifts, abilities and possibilities fade away from spiritual thirst, and the fair virgins and strong young men die of thirst! They realize the sin of Samaria, and seek the strange gods in the north, "Dan," and in the south, "the way of Beersheba," "even they shall fall, and never rise up again" [14].

8.7.1.en: It is a terrible famine in which the soul seeks spiritual satisfaction and does not find it, not because God has deprived it, but because, through its multiplied sins and its unwillingness to repent, it loses its perception of the word of God as the bread of life.

8.7.2.en: Would that we might always enjoy the word of the Lord, of which the Master Himself says: "The words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life" (Jn 6:63). And St. John Chrysostom says: [(The word of God) is the food of the soul, its adornment, and its pledge; in not hearing it there is famine and deprivation.]

8.7.3.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa sees that when God threatens the wicked with a famine that is not of bread and a thirst that is not for water, He on the other hand grants His children in Paradise fruits fitting for His promises, not material fruits and material water but the bread of life and the fountain of life.

8.7.4.en: This is the living bread with which we must be satisfied and which we must offer to our hungry brethren, as Joseph offered wheat in the midst of the famine to his father, his mother, his brothers, and to strangers also. In this sense St. Gregory of Nazianzus called St. Basil "the second Joseph," who saved Egypt from the famine by his wise management, offering the bread of angels on which souls hungry for God feed. He declared that he offered food that is not consumed but remains forever giving life.

8.7.5.en: And when St. Gregory of Nazianzus spoke to the delegation coming from Egypt with a shipment of grain, he said: [You have brought with you a remedy not for the famine of bread and the quenching of thirst with water, for such a famine is not frightening and its remedy is easy, but you are treating the famine of hearing the word of the Lord, which is truly more dangerous and whose remedy is very hard at the present time because of the increasing evil and the scarcity of genuine hearers.]

8.7.6.en: Then let us return to the Lord, so that we do not remain in such a famine, wandering from sea to sea, from place to place, while the fair or good virgins and young men faint for thirst [13].

8.7.7.en: We said that the fair virgins are the senses which God gave us good and beautiful; if we deprive ourselves of the word of God they wither and become ugly and evil, having no oil to enjoy the eternal wedding (Mt 25). By deprivation of the word of God, through the famine, our good virgins turn into foolish virgins who lose their light through their fleshly thoughts.
